idiom_name: @Injectable() service class resolved by the framework's container
implementation_notes: With a framework in play the container is the library part: decorate the coarse workflow class with @Injectable(), register it in the module's providers array, and let constructor injection supply the fine-grained services; Nest resolves them from emitted type metadata, and request-scoped providers give the facade a per-request instance when the workflow needs one. The framework substitutes for the EJB container's lifecycle and transaction services (interceptors, TypeORM/Prisma transaction callbacks, request-scoped context), while the class remains the coarse boundary. Note the type-erasure constraint: interfaces cannot be injection tokens, so DI targets are classes or explicit tokens. Keep this variant when several entry points share the workflow and the container should own its lifetime.
pitfalls: Types are erased at runtime: an interface cannot be a DI token, so injection must target a class or an explicit @Inject('TOKEN') provider or the container fails at bootstrap.
Request-scoped providers bubble their scope upward; injecting one into a default (singleton) facade silently changes the facade's lifetime or throws during bootstrap.
Parallel calls on a shared repository instance can interleave transactions on one connection; keep one unit of work per workflow invocation.

variants.name: Framework-free service module exporting coarse async functions
variants.idiom_name: module of exported async use-case functions (type-only contracts)
variants.implementation_notes: Framework-free TypeScript uses the module as the facade: services/orders.ts imports the fine-grained modules and exports one async function per use case with explicit request/response types, and the package's exports map keeps the internals unimportable from outside. TypeScript adds what JavaScript lacks here - typed coarse contracts (import type { PlaceOrderRequest }) documented at the boundary - while the structure stays the functional composition of functions rather than a class. Choose this shape when no container is present or when the DI indirection outweighs the wiring it removes; the transaction boundary then belongs either to a repository-level wrapper or to the framework adapter that calls the function.
pitfalls: Module-level state (a shared client, a cache map) becomes a process-wide singleton shared by every request and every test in the same process.

Without a container the transaction boundary is implicit: the coarse function must either open the unit of work itself or document that the caller does, or partial writes leak out of failed workflows.
